# Cupertino

> MCP servers for the Apple apps already on your Mac — Mail, Notes, Reminders, Calendar,
> Contacts, Messages and Safari — and the signed menu-bar app that holds their one Full Disk Access
> grant instead of handing it to every editor.

Unofficial. Not affiliated with Apple. macOS 26 or later, and macOS only. Shipped at 1.0.0, and at
1.2.0 as of August 2026: the signed app ships from GitHub releases. The `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-*`
packages are MIT, and apart from `-core` they are not on npm yet — the app carries them.

## The argument

- Full Disk Access is a single, indivisible grant, and it lands on whatever process launched the
  server — your editor or your terminal, never Mail itself. Granting it to Mail.app does nothing.
- Four MCP hosts therefore mean four whole-disk grants. Cupertino is one signed, notarized app that
  holds it once, and the bundle identifier `io.mgcrea.cupertino` is the TCC identity, so the grant
  survives updates.
- The grant buys speed as well as reach: the same Mail search is 74,000 ms over Apple Events and
  97 ms off the Envelope Index.
- Write tools are not merely refused when writes are off — they are never registered, because MCP
  clients cache the tool list.

## Surfaces

- Mail — 18 tools (10 always registered, 8 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-mail`
- Notes — 12 tools (7 always registered, 5 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-notes`
- Reminders — 11 tools (6 always registered, 5 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-reminders`
- Calendar — 9 tools (6 always registered, 3 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-calendar`
- Contacts — 7 tools (5 always registered, 2 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-contacts`. Turns a
  phone number or an email address into a name, which is what makes the Messages server readable.
  Its reads need no Automation grant — only the two write tools reach Apple Events. There is
  no delete tool because Contacts' scripting dictionary has no delete command.
- Messages — 6 tools (5 always registered, 1 write-gated). `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-messages`. iMessage,
  SMS and RCS out of chat.db, with names resolved through Contacts. The only surface with no read
  fallback at all: every read through Messages' own scripting interface fails, so Full Disk Access
  is mandatory rather than an upgrade. It is also the only one where Apple Events is a write lane
  and nothing else — `send` is the single mutating command the dictionary offers, and with writes
  off no Apple Event is ever sent. Roughly 3% of messages across all history keep their text only
  in an archived blob that SQL cannot reach, and since Apple stopped writing the plain column in
  early 2026 that is ~100% of recent ones, so the server decodes them.
- Safari — 6 tools, all always registered. `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-safari`. History, live tabs, bookmarks
  and the Reading List, read-only. The one surface whose two lanes see almost disjoint things rather
  than the same thing at different speeds: Apple Events sees what is open right now, the file lane
  sees everything except that. `list_tabs` is the only tool in the bundle that works with no Full
  Disk Access at all — it needs an Automation grant instead. There is no write tool and no
  `do JavaScript` tool: the latter needs a developer-menu toggle that is not a TCC grant and whose
  state cannot be read, so shipping it would mean reporting a healthy surface whose most powerful
  capability silently fails.
- Maps — 8 tools, all read-only. Favourites, Guides, recents and places filed in no Guide, with coordinates. `@mgcrea/mcp-apple-maps`

## Price

- $14.99 once, covering every 1.x release. Not a subscription, nothing lapses, and 2.0 is a separate
  purchase. EU buyers are quoted and charged €14.99, VAT included — that is not a conversion of the
  dollar figure, which is quoted tax-exclusive.
- There is no price ladder and no announced rise. There was one — three rungs tied to surfaces
  shipping — and every rung came due and was held: Calendar, Contacts, Messages and Safari all landed
  without moving the price. All seven surfaces now cost $14.99. If a rise ever happens it is
  announced beforehand and never applied to a licence already sold.
- A 30-minute trial, started by pressing a button and never armed on its own. Every surface at full
  function, with the write toggles behaving exactly as they will after paying. It is held in memory
  and never written to disk, so quitting and reopening starts another one; nothing prevents that and
  nothing pretends to. When it closes, the servers it started are stopped — refusing only new
  connections would not close it, since an MCP host opens one stdio connection and holds it for the
  life of the editor.
- The trial answers whether Cupertino works against your mail. The 30-day refund answers whether it
  was worth the money. They are different questions and both are available.
- The servers are MIT and run on their own with no key at all. The app is a different matter: its
  source is public and readable, but any build of it — yours or ours — asks for a licence key. A
  licence buys the signed and notarized binary and the upkeep, not access to the source.
- The licence key is verified offline. There is no account, no login and no phone-home. The app
  makes exactly one network connection, the update check, and only once you have turned it on or
  pressed Check Now; it reads one file and sends no identifier. Everything here is checked in CI
  against the built binary, including that automatic checks are off in the shipped bundle.
